section.title: Joseph Sold
section.sectionRationale: The account of Jacob now narrows to Joseph, the favored son whose dreams of rule enrage his brothers. Envy hardens into a plot; Joseph is stripped, thrown into a pit, and sold into Egypt, while his father is left to mourn a son he believes is dead.
section.thesis: Human envy and betrayal do their worst against the beloved dreamer, yet the very act that seems to bury God's purpose becomes the hidden road by which He will save the family, and the world, foreshadowing a greater beloved Son.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the favored son and his dreams; the murderous plot at Dothan; Joseph sold to the traders; and Jacob's inconsolable mourning.

units.label: The favored son and his dreams
units.note: loved, hated, and dreaming of rule

verses.text: Now Jacob lived in the land where his father had resided, the land of Canaan.

This is the account of Jacob. When Joseph was seventeen years old, he was tending the flock with his brothers, the sons of his father’s wives Bilhah and Zilpah, and he brought their father a bad report about them.
Now Israel loved Joseph more than his other sons, because Joseph had been born to him in his old age; so he made him a {{ketonet|robe of many colors}}.
When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father loved him more than any of them, they {{sane|hated}} him and could not speak a kind word to him.
Then Joseph had a {{chalom|dream}}, and when he told it to his brothers, they hated him even more.
He said to them, “Listen to this dream I had:
We were binding sheaves of grain in the field, and suddenly my sheaf rose and stood upright, while your sheaves gathered around and bowed down to mine.”
“Do you intend to reign over us?” his brothers asked. “Will you actually rule us?” So they hated him even more because of his dream and his statements.
Then Joseph had another dream and told it to his brothers. “Look,” he said, “I had another dream, and this time the sun and moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me.”
He told his father and brothers, but his father rebuked him and said, “What is this dream that you have had? Will your mother and brothers and I actually come and bow down to the ground before you?”
And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept in mind what he had said.
Some time later, Joseph’s brothers had gone to pasture their father’s flocks near Shechem.
Israel said to him, “Are not your brothers pasturing the flocks at Shechem? Get ready; I am sending you to them.” “I am ready,” Joseph replied.
Then Israel told him, “Go now and see how your brothers and the flocks are faring, and bring word back to me.” So he sent him off from the Valley of Hebron. And when Joseph arrived in Shechem,
a man found him wandering in the field and asked, “What are you looking for?”
“I am looking for my brothers,” Joseph replied. “Can you please tell me where they are pasturing their flocks?”
“They have moved on from here,” the man answered. “I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’” So Joseph set out after his brothers and found them at Dothan.
Now Joseph’s brothers saw him in the distance, and before he arrived, they plotted to kill him.
“Here comes that dreamer!” they said to one another.
“Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. We can say that a vicious animal has devoured him. Then we shall see what becomes of his dreams!”
When Reuben heard this, he tried to rescue Joseph from their hands. “Let us not take his life,” he said.
“Do not shed his blood. Throw him into this pit in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him.” Reuben said this so that he could rescue Joseph from their hands and return him to his father.
So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe, the robe of many colors he was wearing,
and they took him and threw him into the pit. Now the pit was empty, with no water in it.
And as they sat down to eat a meal, they looked up and saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were carrying spices, balm, and myrrh on their way down to Egypt.
Then Judah said to his brothers, “What profit will we gain if we kill our brother and cover up his blood?
Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay a hand on him; for he is our brother, our own flesh.” And they agreed.
So when the Midianite traders passed by, his brothers pulled Joseph out of the pit and sold him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt.
When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not there, he tore his clothes,
returned to his brothers, and said, “The boy is gone! What am I going to do?”
Then they took Joseph’s robe, slaughtered a young goat, and dipped the robe in its blood.
They sent the robe of many colors to their father and said, “We found this. Examine it to see whether it is your son’s robe or not.”
His father recognized it and said, “It is my son’s robe! A vicious animal has devoured him. Joseph has surely been torn to pieces!”
Then Jacob tore his clothes, put sackcloth around his waist, and mourned for his son many days.
All his sons and daughters tried to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. “No,” he said. “I will go down to {{sheol|Sheol}} mourning for my son.” So his father wept for him.
Meanwhile, the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.

ketonet.gloss: A special tunic, possibly long-sleeved or richly ornamented, the robe of many colors. It marks Joseph as his father's favorite and, some suggest, as the one set over his brothers. The brothers strip it from him and dip it in blood, so the badge of love becomes the token of his supposed death.

sane.gloss: To hate. The word is repeated as the brothers' hatred deepens with each of Joseph's words and dreams, verses 4, 5, and 8. Their hatred, born of envy at their father's favor, is the engine that drives them toward betrayal, echoing the hatred that would later meet the beloved Son.

chalom.gloss: A dream. Dreams frame the whole Joseph story, from these boyhood visions of sheaves and stars to Pharaoh's dreams in Egypt. Here they reveal God's purpose that Joseph will one day rule and be bowed to, a purpose the brothers try in vain to kill.

sheol.gloss: The grave, the realm of the dead. Jacob says he will go down to Sheol still mourning, a picture of grief that expects no comfort this side of death. It heightens the darkness of the moment, for the reader knows the son Jacob mourns is alive and being carried toward God's purpose.

basic.context: The story now follows Joseph, Jacob's favorite son. His special robe and his dreams of his family bowing to him stir his brothers' hatred. When he is sent to check on them, they seize him, throw him into a pit, and sell him to traders bound for Egypt. They deceive Jacob into thinking Joseph is dead.
basic.hermeneutics: The key question is where God is in all this evil. He is never mentioned in the chapter, yet the whole story turns on His hidden hand. What the brothers mean for harm, God is quietly bending toward salvation, as later chapters will reveal.
basic.originalLanguages: The robe of many colors marks Joseph as favored. The word hated is repeated as the brothers' envy grows. Dreams, which frame the whole Joseph story, reveal God's purpose that Joseph will rule. And Jacob speaks of going down to Sheol, the grave, in unending grief for a son who is in fact alive.
basic.typology: Joseph is a striking picture of Christ: the beloved son, sent by his father to his brothers, rejected and stripped, sold for silver, and given up for dead, yet destined to be exalted and to save. Judah's role in the sale even echoes the later betrayal for silver.
basic.christ: Like Joseph, Jesus is the Father's beloved Son, sent to His own who hated Him, betrayed for pieces of silver, stripped of His garment, and handed over to seeming death. And like Joseph, He is raised to rule and to save the very ones who wronged Him.
basic.god: God is unseen but sovereign. Through envy, betrayal, and a slave sale, He is beginning to work the rescue of Jacob's family from famine. The chapter teaches that God's purposes advance even through, and especially through, the sins of others.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 105 says God sent Joseph ahead as a slave to preserve life. Genesis 50 states plainly that what the brothers meant for evil, God meant for good. Acts 7 and the Gospels echo the pattern of a rejected deliverer.
basic.oneStory: This is the beginning of the road that carries Israel down into Egypt. A beloved son is betrayed and sold, seemingly the end of God's promise, but it is the hidden way God will preserve the covenant family and point ahead to the beloved Son who saves through rejection.

context.literary:
Genesis 37:2 opens the last and longest of the book's family accounts, 'This is the account of Jacob,' which runs to the end of Genesis. The heading names Jacob, but the story that follows belongs mostly to his sons, and above all to Joseph and Judah. Chapter 37 is the overture. It introduces the conflict, the dreams that will drive the plot, and the question the rest of the story answers: will the brothers' hatred have the last word, or will the dreams?

The chapter moves in three scenes. Verses 2 to 11 are set at home, and their engine is repetition: the brothers 'hated him,' verse 4, 'hated him even more,' verse 5, 'hated him even more,' verse 8, and finally 'were jealous of him,' verse 11. Verses 12 to 30 take place in the field, from Shechem to Dothan, and they climb to the pit and the sale. Verses 31 to 35 return home with the robe and end in Jacob's grief. Verse 36 is a coda that turns the camera to Egypt and leaves the reader holding a secret Jacob does not know: the boy is alive.

The storyteller works with doubled elements. There are two dreams, two brothers who try to stop the killing, Reuben and Judah, two names for the traders, and two uses of the robe, first as a sign of love and then as evidence of death. Doubling runs through the whole Joseph story, with pairs of dreams again in chapters 40 and 41.

The chapter also launches a chain of garments and deceptions. The brothers deceive their father with a goat and a garment, verse 31, just as Jacob once deceived his own father with goat skins and Esau's clothing, Genesis 27:15-16. Chapter 38 will use a garment and a pledge to unmask Judah, and chapter 39 will turn Joseph's cloak into false evidence. Clothes tell the truth and lie in turn throughout these chapters.
context.historical:
Joseph is seventeen, verse 2, and the family is living in the Valley of Hebron, verse 14, in the south of the hill country. The brothers have taken the flocks some fifty miles north to Shechem, a place with ugly memories after Simeon and Levi's massacre there, Genesis 34:25, and then on to Dothan, a town on the route north of Shechem that appears again in Elisha's day, 2 Kings 6:13. Pastoral families regularly moved flocks long distances in search of grazing, and a father sending a son to check on them is natural.

The caravan of verse 25 travels the route from Gilead, east of the Jordan, down to Egypt, carrying 'spices, balm, and myrrh.' Balm from Gilead was proverbial, and aromatic resins were in steady demand in Egypt for medicine, perfume and embalming. Both Ishmael and Midian were sons of Abraham, Genesis 25:1-2 and 25:12, so the traders who buy Joseph are distant kin of the brothers. Judges 8:24 later calls Midianites 'Ishmaelites,' which shows the names could overlap for desert traders.

The price was 'twenty shekels of silver,' verse 28, which the BSB footnote gives as about eight ounces. It matches the valuation later set in the law for a male between five and twenty years old, Leviticus 27:5, a fair market figure for a youth.

The empty cistern of verse 24 is the kind of bottle shaped pit cut into rock to catch winter rain; dry, it made a prison from which no one could climb out, as Jeremiah later found, Jeremiah 38:6.

Potiphar is 'captain of the guard,' verse 36. A closely related title is given to Nebuchadnezzar's officer Nebuzaradan, 2 Kings 25:8, and the noun behind 'guard' is related to the word for a cook or butcher, 1 Samuel 9:23, which suggests an office that began at the royal table and grew into command of the king's bodyguard. Jacob's torn clothes and sackcloth, verse 34, are the standard signs of mourning in the ancient Near East.
context.canonical:
The chapter is recalled across the Old Testament. Psalm 105:16-19 retells it as God's own plan: 'He sent a man before them, Joseph, sold as a slave,' and it adds a detail Genesis does not give, that 'they bruised his feet with shackles.' The psalm then says he waited 'until his prediction came true,' linking the dreams of this chapter to their fulfilment. Joseph himself later interprets the whole event in Genesis 45:5 and 50:20, and the brothers' own conscience goes back to the pit in Genesis 42:21, 'We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us.' That plea is not recorded in chapter 37; the narrator saves it for the moment of guilt.

The dreams are fulfilled step by step: the brothers bow 'with their faces to the ground' in Genesis 42:6, and again in 43:26 and 44:14. The robe of many colors reappears only in the story of David's daughter Tamar, 2 Samuel 13:18-19, another favoured child whose robe is torn after violence within the family.

In the New Testament Stephen puts the chapter at the centre of his speech: 'Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him,' Acts 7:9. Stephen's pattern is that Israel has repeatedly rejected the deliverers God sent, Joseph, then Moses, Acts 7:35, then the Righteous One, Acts 7:52. Jesus' parable of the tenants echoes the brothers' words closely: 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him,' Matthew 21:38, beside 'Come now, let us kill him,' Genesis 37:20. The Gospels record that the chief priests handed Jesus over 'out of envy,' Matthew 27:18 and Mark 15:10, the very motive of verse 11. Hebrews 11:22 remembers Joseph's faith at the end of his life, the other end of the road this chapter begins.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The narrator wants Israel to see its own tribes at their worst. These brothers are the fathers of the twelve tribes, and Israel is not allowed to remember them as heroes. Envy, deceit, cruelty and indifference, eating a meal beside a pit where their brother is crying, verse 25, are part of the nation's founding story. The chapter teaches that the people of God are not chosen because they are good.

He also wants the hearers to learn how God works. The chapter never names God, yet it is shaped around dreams that only God could give and fulfil. The reader is being trained to read history the way Joseph will later read it, Genesis 50:20: human evil is real and fully guilty, but it does not defeat God's intention.

Finally, the chapter sets up a moral question that the rest of the story resolves. Will these brothers repeat the pattern, or will they change? The next time a favoured son of Rachel stands in danger, Benjamin in chapter 44, Judah, who proposed selling Joseph, offers himself as a slave in the boy's place, Genesis 44:33. The first hearers were meant to watch for that change and to see in it that God's purpose includes not only rescue from famine but the transformation of the family.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Nearly everything in this chapter is description, and much of it is description of sin. Jacob's open favouritism, Joseph's bad report and his unguarded telling of the dreams, the brothers' plot, the sale and the lie are all recorded, not commended. Genesis has already shown favouritism breaking a family, Genesis 25:28 and 29:30, and it shows it again here.

What carries forward is wisdom learned by watching. Parents are warned by Jacob's example. Those who are gifted or favoured are warned by Joseph's naivety. Everyone is warned by the progress of envy from resentment to hatred to the willingness to kill, which James describes: 'where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every evil practice,' James 3:16.

The chapter also teaches by what it withholds. God's purpose is not an excuse for the brothers. Genesis 42:21-22 has them confess guilt, and Genesis 50:20 holds both truths together: 'you intended' evil, 'God intended' good. Believers today may trust God's providence in suffering without ever using it to excuse wrongdoing.

debates.question: Who actually sold Joseph, the Ishmaelites or the Midianites?

views.label: One caravan, two names
views.case: The terms Ishmaelite and Midianite are used interchangeably for the same traveling merchants, as in Judges 8:24, where Midianite enemies are said to be Ishmaelites, so the brothers sold Joseph to a single caravan described by both names. Genesis 39:1 says Potiphar bought him from the Ishmaelites, while Genesis 37:36 says the Midianites sold him, which fits one group called by both names.

views.label: A layered account
views.case: Some read a deliberately compressed telling in which Midianites drew Joseph up and the Ishmaelites carried him to Egypt, and critical scholars posit combined sources; even so, the canonical text presents one coherent event, and Joseph later says plainly to his brothers, 'the one you sold into Egypt,' Genesis 45:4.

debates.bearing: Either way the outcome is the same: Joseph's brothers are responsible for handing him over, and he is carried to Egypt, where God will place him to save many lives.

debates.question: Is Joseph partly to blame for his brothers' hatred?

views.label: An immature and provocative youth
views.case: Joseph brings a 'bad report' about his brothers, verse 2, wears the robe that marks him above them, and tells his dreams twice, the second time even to his father, who rebukes him, verse 10. On this reading he is a spoiled seventeen year old whose tactlessness fed the fire, and the years of slavery and prison are part of God's shaping of his character.

views.label: An innocent bearer of God's word
views.case: The narrator never blames Joseph. The dreams come from God, as their fulfilment shows, and Joseph simply reports them. The report in verse 2 need not be malicious, and the brothers' hatred is traced to Jacob's favouritism, verse 4, and to envy, verse 11. Psalm 105:19 says the word of the LORD proved him right.

debates.bearing: The text allows that Joseph was young and unguarded without making him the cause of what follows. Whatever his immaturity, the guilt of the plot lies with the brothers, and the dreams are God's, not Joseph's invention. The later Joseph, who weeps over his brothers, shows the fruit of a hard school.

study.originalLanguages:
The 'robe of many colors' in verse 3 is kethoneth passim. Kethoneth is the ordinary word for a tunic, the garment God made for Adam and Eve, Genesis 3:21. The second word is the difficult one. The Septuagint rendered it 'many colored,' which the BSB follows, but its footnote gives another sense, 'a robe with long sleeves,' reaching to the wrists and ankles. Either way it was not work clothing. Elsewhere the phrase appears only in 2 Samuel 13:18-19, where it is the garment worn by 'the king's virgin daughters,' and David's daughter Tamar tears it in her grief. The robe marks Joseph as set apart, and the brothers strip it off in verse 23 before they strip him of everything else.

Verse 4 says the brothers 'could not speak a kind word to him,' literally they could not speak to him in shalom, peace. Ten verses later Jacob sends Joseph 'to see how your brothers and the flocks are faring,' literally to see the shalom of his brothers, verse 14. The family that has no shalom toward Joseph is the family Joseph is sent to check the shalom of. The narrator lets the word do the work of irony.

When Jacob calls, Joseph answers 'I am ready,' verse 13, the Hebrew hinneni, 'here I am.' It is the answer Abraham gave when God called him before the testing of Genesis 22:1, and Isaac gave when his father spoke on Moriah, Genesis 22:7. Joseph is the willing son sent by a father, and the word places him in that line.

The brothers call him 'that dreamer,' verse 19, but the Hebrew is more cutting: ba'al hachalomoth, 'master of dreams' or 'lord of dreams.' Ba'al can mean owner or lord, and the brothers use it with sarcasm. The one they mock as a lord of dreams will in fact become lord of Egypt, Genesis 45:8, because he is truly master of dreams by God's gift, Genesis 41:16.

In verse 32 the brothers say to Jacob, 'Examine it,' hakker na, 'please recognize.' Jacob 'recognized it,' verse 33. The same phrase returns in Genesis 38:25-26, when Tamar says to Judah 'Please examine' his seal and staff, and Judah 'recognized them.' The verb binds the two chapters together. Judah, who helped deceive his father with a garment, is himself unmasked with a personal item, and the lesson is not lost on him.

Finally, Jacob says, 'I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son,' verse 35. This is the first time Sheol, the realm of the dead, is named in the Bible. It returns as a refrain in Jacob's mouth, Genesis 42:38 and 44:29, and it belongs to a wider pattern of going down in these chapters: the caravan goes down to Egypt, verse 25, Judah goes down from his brothers, Genesis 38:1, and Joseph is brought down to Egypt, Genesis 39:1. Every descent seems to be toward death, and every one of them is toward the place where God will preserve life.

typology.type: Joseph, the beloved son sent by his father to his brothers
typology.fulfillment: Jacob loves Joseph above the others and sends him from Hebron to find his brothers, and Joseph answers 'here I am.' The Father's voice over Jesus says 'This is My beloved Son,' Matthew 3:17, and the Son is sent into the world, John 3:17. Jesus' own parable draws the pattern: the owner sends 'my beloved son,' and the tenants say 'This is the heir. Let us kill him,' Luke 20:13-14. The escalation is that Joseph did not know what awaited him, while Jesus came knowing He would be rejected. Joseph's naivety and his bad report find no counterpart in the sinless Son.

typology.type: Joseph hated without cause and handed over out of envy
typology.fulfillment: The brothers' hatred grows until 'they were jealous of him,' verse 11, and Stephen names envy as the reason they sold him, Acts 7:9. Pilate 'knew it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over,' Mark 15:10. Jesus applied the psalm to Himself: 'They hated Me without reason,' John 15:25, citing Psalm 69:4. The escalation is that Joseph's rejection saved a family and a region from famine, while Christ's rejection is the means by which the world is reconciled to God. The type falls short in that Joseph's rejection was not chosen by him as an offering.

typology.type: Joseph stripped, sold for silver and given up for dead
typology.fulfillment: The brothers strip Joseph of his robe, sell him for twenty pieces of silver on Judah's proposal, and present his bloodied robe as proof of death. Jesus was sold by Judas, whose name is the Greek form of Judah, for thirty pieces of silver, Matthew 26:15, stripped of His garments, Matthew 27:28, and the soldiers cast lots for His seamless tunic, John 19:23-24. The pattern is striking but the Gospels do not quote Genesis 37 at these points, so it is an echo rather than a declared fulfilment. The escalation is that Joseph only seemed dead, while Christ truly died and truly rose.

typology.type: The pit, a descent that leads to exaltation
typology.fulfillment: Joseph is thrown into a waterless pit, then carried down to Egypt, and Jacob speaks of going down to Sheol. Yet the descent is the road to Joseph's rule over Egypt, Genesis 41:40. Zechariah 9:11 later uses the image of 'prisoners from the waterless pit' released through the blood of the covenant. Christ descended into death and was then exalted 'to the highest place,' Philippians 2:9. The escalation is that Christ went all the way into death that Joseph only approached, and His exaltation brings His people up with Him, Ephesians 2:6.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ most clearly by pattern, and the New Testament itself traces the pattern. Stephen's speech in Acts 7 is the key. He tells Joseph's story, 'the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him,' Acts 7:9, and then Moses' story, 'whom they had rejected,' Acts 7:35, and he ends with the Righteous One whom his hearers betrayed and murdered, Acts 7:52. For Stephen, Joseph is the first in a line of rejected deliverers, and the line finds its climax in Jesus. The brothers did not recognize Joseph when they saw him again, Genesis 42:8, and Stephen notes that it was 'on their second visit' that Joseph revealed his identity, Acts 7:13.

The correspondences are real. The beloved son of the father, Genesis 37:3, points to the Son of whom the Father says, 'This is My beloved Son,' Matthew 3:17. The son sent by his father to his brothers answers to the Son who 'came to His own, and His own did not receive Him,' John 1:11. The brothers' words, 'Come now, let us kill him,' Genesis 37:20, are echoed by the tenants in Jesus' parable, 'Come, let us kill him and take his inheritance,' Matthew 21:38. Envy moves the brothers, Genesis 37:11, and envy moves the chief priests, Matthew 27:18. Joseph is stripped of his robe and sold for silver; Jesus is stripped and sold for silver. The one who proposes the sale is Judah, and the one who betrays Jesus bears the Greek form of the same name.

The chapter also leads to Christ by contrast. Joseph goes down to Egypt without choosing it; Jesus 'gave Himself up for us,' Ephesians 5:2. Jacob grieves a son who is in fact alive; the Father 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32, knowing exactly what the giving would cost. Joseph's dreams were about his family bowing to him; Jesus' exaltation brings not only bowing but reconciliation, 'every knee' bowing, Philippians 2:10, and brothers welcomed at His table.

And it leads to Christ by the theme it opens: God's purpose running under human evil. The sale of Joseph is the start of the road to Genesis 50:20, 'what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good.' Peter uses the same double explanation of the cross: Jesus was 'delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge, and you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death,' Acts 2:23. The brothers remain guilty, and so do those who crucified Jesus, and in both cases God turns the worst act into the means of saving many.

The pattern should not be pushed into every detail. The robe is not a coded symbol of Christ's divinity, and the twenty shekels are not a riddle about the thirty. What makes Joseph a genuine type is the shape of his whole story, rejected by his brothers, brought down to seeming death, raised to the right hand of the throne, and becoming the saviour of the very ones who sold him.
study.god:
God is not named once in Genesis 37, and that absence is part of what the chapter teaches about Him. The narrator, who has spoken freely of God appearing to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, now tells a story in which God does not speak, appear or intervene. Yet the whole chapter moves under His hand. The dreams are His, as later events show. The 'man' who finds Joseph wandering near Shechem, verses 15 to 17, and sends him on to Dothan, arrives at exactly the moment the story needs him. The caravan passes just when Judah is looking for an alternative to murder. None of this is labelled providence; the reader discovers it by looking back from Genesis 45:5 and 50:20.

The chapter therefore shapes the doctrine of providence. God governs not only through miracles but through ordinary events, a family quarrel, a passing caravan, a traveller's directions. Psalm 105:17 describes the same events from God's side: 'He sent a man before them.' What the brothers did as a crime, God did as a sending.

The chapter also holds together God's sovereignty and human responsibility without explaining one away. The brothers are fully guilty; Reuben later says 'we must account for his blood,' Genesis 42:22, echoing God's words to Cain about a brother's blood crying from the ground, Genesis 4:10. Yet God is not a bystander to their guilt. He is at work in it, as Joseph later says: 'you intended... God intended,' Genesis 50:20. God does not make them sin, and their sin does not escape His purpose.

God's faithfulness to His word appears in the dreams. The sheaves and stars announce a future no one in the family wants, and it comes to pass. Jacob 'kept in mind what he had said,' verse 11, a phrase that anticipates the way Mary 'treasured up all these things in her heart,' Luke 2:51. God's word waits, often for years, but it does not fail.

The chapter shows, too, that God allows His people to suffer deeply for a long time. Jacob refuses comfort and expects to die mourning. God does not step in to tell him the truth. Those who worship this God learn that His silence is not His absence, and that His purposes are larger than a single generation's grief.

For worship, this chapter teaches trust in the dark. It gives no easy comfort, but it gives the reader a vantage point Jacob did not have: the God who is unseen in chapter 37 is the God who, by chapter 50, has turned every evil in it to 'the lives of many people.'

crossReferences.note: Joseph's final word on the events that begin in this chapter: 'what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good.' The verse keeps both agents in view. The brothers' plot in Genesis 37:18-28 is truly evil, and God's purpose running through it is truly good.

Joseph names the deed plainly, 'the one you sold into Egypt,' and then tells his brothers not to be distressed, 'because it was to save lives that God sent me before you.' The sale of Genesis 37:28 is reinterpreted as God's sending without being excused.

Twenty years later the brothers' conscience goes back to the pit: 'We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us.' Genesis 37 does not record Joseph's cries; the narrator holds them back until the moment of guilt. Reuben adds that they must now account for his blood.

Rebekah dressed Jacob in Esau's clothes and covered his hands with goat skins to deceive Isaac. In Genesis 37:31-33 Jacob's sons use a goat and a garment to deceive Jacob. The deceiver is deceived by the same means he once used.

The psalm retells Joseph's descent as God's own act: God called down famine and 'sent a man before them, Joseph, sold as a slave.' It adds that his feet were bruised with shackles, and that he waited until the word of the LORD proved him right, linking the dreams of Genesis 37 to their fulfilment.

Stephen says the patriarchs sold Joseph because they were jealous, 'But God was with him and rescued him from all his troubles.' Stephen supplies the divine side that Genesis 37 leaves silent, and he uses Joseph as the first of Israel's rejected deliverers.

In Jesus' parable the tenants see the owner's son and say, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him.' The words closely echo Genesis 37:20, and the parable, like the chapter, is about a beloved son sent by his father and rejected by those who should have received him.

Pilate knew 'it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over.' Envy is also the motive Genesis 37:11 names in Joseph's brothers. In both stories jealousy of one favoured by the father leads to his being handed over to foreigners.

Judas asks what the priests will give him to hand Jesus over, and they set out thirty pieces of silver. In Genesis 37:26-28 Judah asks 'What profit will we gain?' and Joseph is sold for twenty shekels. The echo is in the bargain as well as in the name.

The one other passage where the 'robe of many colors' appears, worn by David's daughter Tamar as a mark of royal status. As in Genesis 37, a favoured child in a troubled household wears the robe, and it becomes a sign of the violence done to her within her own family.

Judah, who proposed selling Joseph, offers to stay as a slave in place of Benjamin. It is the reversal of Genesis 37:26-27. Where he once sold a brother into slavery, he now offers himself as a slave so that a brother may go free.

Peter explains the cross with the same double account Genesis gives of Joseph's sale: Jesus was delivered up 'by God's set plan and foreknowledge,' and 'you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death.' Divine purpose and human guilt stand side by side.

study.oneStory:
In the Bible's larger story this chapter carries the promise into its darkest tunnel so far. God had told Abraham that his descendants would be strangers 'in a land that is not their own,' 'enslaved and mistreated four hundred years,' and afterward brought out, Genesis 15:13-14. Genesis 37 is how that begins. A family quarrel in Canaan starts the chain that will bring all of Israel down into Egypt. What looks like the unravelling of the family is the first step of a road God announced before Isaac was born.

The chapter also answers something from the very beginning of the story. The first murder in the Bible was a brother killing a brother out of resentment, Genesis 4:8, and the fall has run through every generation of this family since, Ishmael and Isaac, Esau and Jacob, Leah and Rachel. Here the brothers plan the same crime as Cain. The difference is that God is at work to heal the family and not only to judge it, and the long story that follows ends with brothers reconciled and weeping together.

It sets up much that follows. The descent into Egypt leads to slavery, and slavery to the exodus, which becomes the Bible's great picture of redemption. Joseph's role as a rejected brother who becomes saviour prepares for Moses, rejected by his fellow Israelites before he becomes their deliverer, Exodus 2:14, and above all for Jesus.

In Christ the pattern reaches its fulfilment. The beloved Son was sent by His Father to His own people, hated without cause, sold, stripped and handed over to death, and then raised and exalted, and He saves not only a family but a people from every nation. The rejection that looked like the end of God's purpose was the centre of it.

The new creation completes it. Joseph's brothers finally bowed before him and found mercy instead of vengeance, and the story ends with a family fed and preserved. Revelation pictures the great multitude before the throne of the Lamb who was slain, where 'Never again will they hunger,' Revelation 7:16, and the dreams God gave at the start of the story come true on a scale Joseph never imagined.

quiz.q: What stirred the brothers' hatred of Joseph to the breaking point?

options.text: Their father's favoritism and Joseph's dreams of them bowing to him.
options.note: The robe and the dreams of rule fueled envy into hatred, verses 3 to 11.

options.text: Joseph's cruelty toward them in the fields.
options.note: Joseph brought a bad report, but the text centers the cause on favor and the dreams, not cruelty.

options.text: A dispute over inheritance money.
options.note: Money is not the issue; the envy is over their father's love and Joseph's dreams.

options.text: Joseph refusing to tend the flocks.
options.note: Joseph was tending the flocks and was sent to check on his brothers.

quiz.q: Although God is never named in the chapter, how is He at work?

options.text: He providentially moves Joseph toward Egypt to preserve the family from famine.
options.note: Later Scripture reveals God's hidden hand, Genesis 50:20 and Psalm 105.

options.text: He is absent, having abandoned the family to their sin.
options.note: God's silence is not absence; He is sovereignly guiding events.

options.text: He punishes Joseph for his pride by ending his story.
options.note: Joseph's story is only beginning; God is preserving, not punishing him.

options.text: He miraculously rescues Joseph from the pit at once.
options.note: Joseph is sold into slavery; God's rescue unfolds over years, not instantly.

quiz.q: How is Joseph in this chapter a picture of Christ?

options.text: A beloved son sent to his brothers, rejected, stripped, and sold for silver.
options.note: The pattern mirrors Christ's rejection and betrayal for silver.

options.text: A powerful king who conquers his enemies by force.
options.note: That comes later in a different key; here the likeness is in rejection and suffering.

options.text: A priest offering sacrifices at an altar.
options.note: Joseph is not pictured as a priest here; the parallel is the rejected beloved son.

options.text: A prophet who calls the nations to repent.
options.note: The Christ-parallel in this chapter is suffering and betrayal, not prophetic preaching.

quiz.q: What did the brothers do to deceive their father?

options.text: They dipped Joseph's robe in goat's blood and let Jacob assume he was dead.
options.note: The badge of favor became the token of supposed death, verses 31 to 33.

options.text: They told him plainly that they had sold Joseph.
options.note: They hid the truth; Jacob learns it only years later.

options.text: They claimed Joseph had run away to Egypt.
options.note: They implied a wild animal killed him, not that he fled.

options.text: They said Joseph drowned in a well.
options.note: They said a vicious animal devoured him.

quiz.q: How does this chapter fit the larger biblical story?

options.text: It begins the road into Egypt by which God preserves the covenant family.
options.note: The betrayal is the hidden means of rescue and the setup for the Exodus.

options.text: It marks the failure and end of God's promise to Abraham.
options.note: The promise seems threatened but is in fact being preserved by God.

options.text: It shows that dreams are meaningless distractions.
options.note: The dreams carry God's true purpose and come to pass.

options.text: It concludes the story of Joseph.
options.note: It only begins Joseph's story, which fills the rest of Genesis.

questions: Jacob's favoritism sowed years of pain in his family. Where might partiality, even unintended, be doing quiet damage in your relationships?
The brothers hated Joseph for his dreams and his father's love. How do you handle the envy that rises when someone else seems favored or gifted?
God was working through betrayal that no one could see as good at the time. How does Joseph's story help you trust God in seasons when His hand is hidden?
Joseph foreshadows the beloved Son who saves through rejection. How does seeing Christ in this story deepen your worship of the One who was sold and stripped for you?
Jacob refused to be comforted, certain his son was dead, while Joseph was alive in God's care. Where do you need to hold space for hope in a grief that feels final?

translationNotes.note: Robe of many colors renders a Hebrew phrase of uncertain meaning; it may indicate a long-sleeved or richly ornamented tunic. Either way it marks Joseph as specially favored.
Ishmaelites and Midianites appear to describe the same caravan of traders, used interchangeably here as elsewhere in Scripture; twenty shekels was a customary price for a young slave.
Sheol denotes the grave or realm of the dead, not a place of torment; Jacob means he will grieve until he himself dies.
